Item 1 of the ranked plan is closed, and one recorded number turned out to be wrong.

**The unlock.** The single-atom kernel is exactly κ_ω(τ) = τ^(ω−1)·Ĝ(τ) with Ĝ **holomorphic on |τ| < π**. So the spike that carries half its mass below τ = 2^(−1/ω) belongs in a Gauss–Jacobi *weight*, not in an evaluated quantity. Local coordinates then come for free, nothing underflows, 30 nodes per atom give 40 digits, and the whole assembly runs in double precision — which is what made a registered check possible. The companion identity, using Γ alone,

∫₀^∞ e^(−pτ)κ_ω dτ = π^ω · Γ((a+p)/2)/Γ((b+p)/2) · (p+a)(p−b)/((p+b)(p−a))

matches the assembly to 1.4×10⁻¹³; its two-line Beta-integral proof also pins the opening note's Beta variable as U = e^(−2τ), which sharpens the open Loewner question.

**A correction to the record.** The 17 September margin rows at ω = 0.002 and 0.01 sat beneath that note's own tanh–sinh floor. The true ratios are 1.00108 and 1.00542, not 0.99717 and 1.00109 — confirmed by re-running *the old programme* at 1/h = 26, which converges to 1.005421 against Gauss–Jacobi's 1.005422. Its mass and e₁ rows were always right; the floor lives only in the oscillatory matrix elements. What replaces them is cleaner: the Galerkin excess is exactly linear in ω with slope 0.5394, which is Proposition 2.2's truncation term and nothing else.

**Three horizons.** Strict contraction and the first-order law at log 3, log 5, log 7 — margins from 6.2×10⁻⁸ to 2.1×10⁻²², fourteen orders of magnitude, with the deviation linear in ω at each. Past log 7 the nested defect stops being a refinement: at log 11 and log 13 the plain N=24 defect overstates by 5.3× and 16.6×, and nesting in 64 modes recovers it. Carried to N′ = 192 the nested ratio crosses below 1, as Proposition 2.2's limit requires — the old "roughly 1/N′" reading is withdrawn.

**Two new things.** P = (2/ω)Re(I−V)(I+V)⁻¹ is *even* in ω, because K₋ω = 1/K_ω and compression is a homomorphism of the causal algebra; the congruence holds to 10⁻⁴¹. And in one basis, the best phase-matched lattice misses the margin by factors 1.07, 2.19, 0.76 where the transfer — no zero, no lattice — misses by 0.54ω, 1.20ω, 1.85ω. A lattice reproduces the density of the zeros; the transfer reproduces the form.

parts:
Honestly? Less than the ranking implies, and I think you've caught something.

What I wrote down for 1 was: compute c₂ in closed form from 2Q² + [Q,A], compare with the measurement, and thereby get the first validated handle on A — the compressed Hilbert transform plus the odd part of the comb, the one operator in the picture nobody has assembled. That's true, but it's a verification of a proposition I derived myself, at one horizon where everything is already known, and it doesn't bear on the dichotomy. I ranked it first partly because it was within arm's reach of the instrument I'd just built, which is momentum, not judgement.

There is one version of it with teeth, and it isn't the closed form. It's the scaling question. The first-order law is only useful over the range of ω where the second-order term hasn't taken over, and that range is set by c₂/m_L. At log 3 the a-priori bound from the Wilson-lines manuscript allows that ratio to be ~3.7×10³; the measurement gives ~1.6. That's three orders of margin, and it's the reason the transfer-side computation works at ω = 0.1 rather than only at ω = 10⁻⁶. Nobody knows whether that gap survives at log 5 and log 7 or collapses toward the a-priori bound as the margin does. If it survives, the instrument is usable at any horizon whose atoms you're willing to sum; if it collapses, the first-order law becomes a statement about a vanishing window and the whole approach is confined to toy horizons. That's an empirical question about the object, it needs no closed form, and it's an afternoon of runs with what already exists. Worth doing, but as a loose end, not as a direction.

**On 3 — I think you're right, and for a reason I underweighted.** It's the only item that can *close* something. The comb is already excluded (far-field transport is a pure delay), the correction is already excluded (forced by unimodularity, no arithmetic in its residues). The archimedean factor is the last piece standing. So a "no" on 3 doesn't just answer a question, it retires the founding proposal of the investigation with three proofs — the name would then record an origin rather than a direction, and that's a publishable negative. A "yes" is obviously better still. Decisive either way is rare; 1 is decisive about nothing. And Proposition 5.2/Remark 5.3 made the target concrete in a way it wasn't two days ago: it's no longer "does some additivity fraction appear somewhere", it's "is e^(−2τ) Beta(a/2, ω)-distributed", which is a specific law to hunt for in the conformal-radius and hitting-time literature.

**On 2, there's more in it than I wrote.** I described it as a dictionary, which undersells it. At ω = ½ the poles of K_{1/2}(p) = ξ(p)/ξ(p+1) sit at p = ρ − 1, all with Re p < 0 — so K_{1/2} is inner on the right half-plane *unconditionally*, and the dichotomy forces contraction at every horizon with no hypothesis at all. That makes ω = ½ the single point where the conclusion the whole program is chasing is already a theorem, and where Lax–Phillips have machinery that ought to prove it. The question worth asking isn't "what is the dictionary" but "does their semigroup estimate, translated, actually deliver the contraction the dichotomy demands — and what exactly breaks as ω comes down off ½?" My own §4.5 already warns that no Eisenstein construction produces the offset 2ω for ω < ½, so the likely answer is that the endpoint is isolated. But knowing *which* object fails to deform, and whether it fails for a structural reason or just because nobody has looked, is worth more than another exclusion.

If it were mine to order: 3 first, because it's cheap to decide and closes a line either way; then 2, framed as "what obstructs deformation off the endpoint"; and the scaling half of 1 folded in as a side run whenever the instrument is already warm. The closed-form c₂ I'd drop unless the scaling measurement turns up something odd.

Both items are settled, and item 3 gave back more than an exclusion.

**The archimedean factor is a horocycle integral in dimension 2ω.** Exactly, for every ω ∈ (0,½]:

K^Γ_ω(p) = ∫_{ℝ^d} |t + i|^{−(p+b)} dt,  d = 2ω

The delay is log|t+i| — the log-modulus along a horocycle, which is the arithmetic coordinate itself. The kernel's prefactor 2π^ω/Γ(ω) is *exactly* the surface area of the unit sphere S^{2ω−1}. So the opening note's "the dimensions are fractional and below one, so there is no sphere and no angle" was half right: there is a sphere, and what's fractional is its dimension. **The shift is half a dimension.** Verified to 1e-15, with the Riesz integral cross-checked by honest quadrature at integer d.

That single fact organizes everything else. d = 2ω takes exactly one integer value in the family's range — d = 1 at ω = ½, the horocycle at the cusp of the modular surface — which is why the endpoint is realized geometrically and the interior is not.

**Item 3 is no**, with three independent proofs: the additivity fraction is independent of the total (so a dimension-b chain cannot see the split b = a + 2ω at all — this kills the mechanism whatever observable you pick); the antipodal exponent of any radial chord law is −½ *for every driving*, because the Loewner drift vanishes at the antipode and only the Itô curvature survives, so a chord law is always Beta(·,½) while the target has both parameters below ½; and the zero-delay singularity is a power law, E[U^q] ~ q^{−ω}, which no interior first-passage time has. The pinned ½ is d/2 at d = 1 — the same quantization, in the other geometry. With the comb and the correction already excluded, **the Loewner proposal closes.**

**Item 2 turned on a fact I hadn't expected to matter so much**: contraction at ω = ½ is *unconditional* — the poles of K_{½}(p) = ξ(p)/ξ(p+1) all sit at Re p ∈ (−1,0). So the family runs from a free endpoint to RH, the whole content is the deformation inward, and what blocks a geometric realization of that deformation is that the Eisenstein offset is a horocycle dimension, hence an integer. That demotes the Lax–Phillips dictionary rather than elevating it: the endpoint conclusion is free, and no semigroup estimate transports inward past the quantization.

**The side run was decisive.** The second-order coefficient is 1.64, 3.33, 1.79 at log 3, 5, 7 against an a-priori κ_L² of 10³, 10¹², 10²² — the sufficient condition is pessimistic by up to 22 orders and the gap widens superexponentially. The first-order law is good at ω ~ 0.1 even at log 7.

Delivered: a second registered check (43 cases, stdlib, replayed — 96 total), the note, and manuscript draft 0.3 at 33 pages with new Sections 4.3 and 4.4 and Proposition 4.10, recorded and snapshotted after reading the new pages. One caveat worth flagging: §4.4 sweeps the observables the proposal named, not every conceivable functional of a chain — only the independence proposition is fully general, and I've labelled it that way.

The new top of the open list is the direction these results point at rather than anything from the old plan: that radial measure |S^{d−1}|r^{d−1}dr is exactly what dimensional regularization and the Bessel–Hankel calculus of index d/2 − 1 give meaning to, so the question is whether the comb and the pole factor also live in that calculus at the same d = 2ω. If they do, the program has a realization of a kind it wasn't looking for; if they don't, the obstruction is pinned at the comb.

I'd been about to execute the rename; I think your alternative is better. Nothing has been moved — the survey was read-only, the tree is untouched.

**My view: leave `loewner` alone and open a new investigation.**

The decisive argument is the sibling convention. Look at the directory: `positive-factorizations`, `topological-susy-bulk`, `arithmetic-ground-state-geometry`, `inverse-bulk-realization`, `source-selection-rules`, `wilson-lines` — and the tree comment says it outright, "approach-specific research packages." Every one is named after the route attempted, not the object studied. `loewner` fits that exactly. A folder that asks "can a Loewner chain build this?" and answers "no, three times, with proofs" is *accurately* named. Renaming it to `markov-part` would make it the only object-named folder in a directory of approach-named ones — and it would quietly erase the fact that a specific, well-motivated proposal was tested and excluded, which is itself a result worth being able to find by name.

There's also a provenance cost that only runs one way. Four hash-pinned snapshots cite `investigations/loewner/...` inside their frozen `references.tex`. Those can't be rewritten, so a rename leaves permanently stale paths inside preserved artifacts. Small, but it's the exact drift this repo's machinery exists to prevent — and it buys navigation convenience that a one-line pointer solves just as well.

And the forward direction really is a different question. "Is the whole transfer one object in the Bessel–Hankel calculus at d = 2ω — does the comb live there too?" is not a continuation of the Loewner proposal; it's a new hypothesis that may well be closed in its turn, exactly as this one was. It should inherit from `loewner` the way `loewner` inherited from `wilson-lines`: an inherited note, a citation, a "relation to the sibling investigations" section. That pattern is already established here.

One real cost of leaving the name, which I'd want to mitigate rather than ignore: the folder's most durable output isn't the exclusions, it's the instrument and the identification — the registered assembly, the Gauss–Jacobi kernel, the contraction margins at three horizons, the Cayley coordinate, and Proposition 4.2. Nobody looking for those would think to open `loewner`. That's fixable with two sentences: one in the program README row and one in the new folder's README, both saying where the assembly lives.

If you want to go ahead, what I'd set up:

- **`investigations/fractional-dimension/`** — approach-named, in convention, and it names the hypothesis being tested rather than a hoped-for result.
- An opening note stating the question precisely: the archimedean factor is ∫_{ℝ^{2ω}}|t+i|^{−(p+b)}dt with radial measure |S^{d−1}|r^{d−1}dr; do the comb K^ζ_ω and the pole factor B_b have expressions in the same calculus at the same d? Either they do — and the transfer is one object rather than three pieces with a dictionary — or they don't, and the obstruction is pinned at the comb.
- `loewner` gets a short closing header: proposal tested, all three factors excluded, continuation in the new folder; and its open list drops to the items that are genuinely still its own.
- The new folder cites the 0.3 manuscript rather than copying anything.

| Factor | In d | At integer d |
|---|---|---|
| archimedean | π^{d/2}Γ(s−d/2)/Γ(s) | ∫_{ℝ^d}\|t+i\|^{−(p+b)}dt — at d=1 the horocycle constant term |
| comb | ζ(2s−d)/ζ(2s), weights J_d(n)/n^{(d+1)/2} | **Jordan totient** — primitive vectors in (ℤ/nℤ)^d; at d=1, φ(n)/n |
| correction | Blaschke pole at p = (d+1)/2 | the pole of ζ(2s−d) at 2s = d+1: the volume term |

So the question I'd posed for the new folder — do the comb and the correction live in the same calculus? — is **yes at the level of formulas**, answered on day one. The shift enters *only* as a dimension: the same d sits in the sphere area, the Γ shift, the ζ offset and the Euler factors, which is why it's worth taking seriously rather than treating as four coincidences. Verified against brute-force primitive-vector counts at d = 1, 2, 3, by Möbius convolution at fractional d, and in exact rationals at d = 1 — with no value of ζ computed anywhere.

That makes the remaining question sharper and more honest than the one I'd drafted: J_d stays a multiplicative function at fractional d but stops counting, ℝ^d stops being a space, and Λ(2s−d)/Λ(2s) stops being anybody's scattering matrix. **Is d a dimension or a parameter** — and if only a parameter, can continuation in it still carry an argument, as in dimensional regularization? I've written the failure criterion in advance: if every candidate object needs d > 1, then the family's range (0,1] is exactly the inaccessible one, and that's the answer.

**Item 1 — which dimension: 2ω, and the factor of two was a coordinate artifact.** τ = log|t+i| is a *Busemann* function on the horocycle, not a distance. The hyperbolic distance is d_H = 2 arcsinh(t/2), and τ ~ r²/2 is a square — so a measure with local exponent r^(2ω−1)dr has local exponent τ^(ω−1)dτ, the two normalized limits differing by exactly 2^(1−ω). In the true half-distance u = d_H/2 (r = 2 sinh u), Lebesgue on ℝ^(2ω) becomes the radial measure of complex hyperbolic space of complex dimension ω, real dimension 2ω: Jacobi parameters (ω−1, 0) with ρ = ω > 0, against (ω/2−1, −1/2) with ρ < 0 in the Busemann coordinate. Only the first has positive ρ and only it accounts for e^(τ/2). The comb, having no radial coordinate at all, fixes d = 2ω independently.

At d = 1 it is 6/π = 2/vol, the classical Eisenstein residue.

So the dictionary closes on one object, and the question sharpens rather than settles: a dimension can be continued, but a rank is a cardinality. The head of the open list is now **is there anything of which J_d and ζ(d+1) are the invariants when d is not an integer?**

The rank question is answered, and the answer has a positive half and a negative half.

**The object at integer d is a lattice of rank d+1 — at every integer, not just d=1.** For a covolume-one lattice L ⊂ ℝ^m, the primitive Epstein zeta E\*_L(s) = Σ_{v prim}|v|^(−2s) satisfies ξ(2s)E\*_L(s) = ξ(m−2s)E\*_{L\*}(m/2−s) — Poisson summation plus the factorization Z_L = ζ(2s)E\*_L. So its reflection ratio is **independent of the lattice**: an invariant of the rank alone. And under the dictionary that ratio is exactly K̃_ω. The transfer's own reflection p ↦ −p *is* the Epstein functional equation s ↦ m/2 − s, which is why it's all-pass on Re p = 0. The previous position — d=1 the only realized point — was too modest; d = 1, 2, 3, … are all realized, as ranks 2, 3, 4, …, just outside the range.

**The cap ω ≤ 1/2 turns out to be a rank cap.** ξ's poles at 0 and 1 put a second pole of the numerator at p = ω − 1/2, inside the closed left half-plane iff m ≤ 2; in the lattice variable it sits where ζ has its own pole. So the family occupies the *first gap* m ∈ (1,2] of the rank sequence, with the modular surface — and RH — at its right endpoint.

**Inside that gap the lattice does not exist.** The point count has a unique interpolation (the q-coefficients of θ^m, polynomial in m), and r_{d+1}(3) = (4/3)(d³−d) is strictly negative for *every* d ∈ (0,1), vanishing only at the endpoints — a single arch below zero, deepest at d = 1/√3. Equivalently θ(it)^(d+1) is not completely monotone anywhere strictly inside: no positive measure, no point set.

So: every piece of the *cusp* data continues positively — J_d > 0, 1/ζ(d+1) ∈ (0,1), the horocycle integral, the unimodularity — and the interior does not. At fractional d there is a **scattering matrix without a space**. The sharpest thing left unexplained is that two positivity statements sit on the same family at the same ω and part company: K̂_ω keeps complete monotonicity, the lattice theta loses it.

New programme `check_epstein_scattering.py`, 327 cases, built on Riemann's theta method in dimension m and cross-checked non-tautologically against direct lattice summation; ζ at real arguments only. The investigation is at 482 cases across four programmes, all deterministic and matching their records; the parent replay still passes at 96. Nine files changed or added, ready for you to commit.
